correctness.rationale: For each finite connected graph realization, the expected update matrix has a positive-definite grounded Laplacian and a unique harmonic limit. Series-parallel reduction gives the exact shortcut endpoint a(t) and piecewise linear profile; direct algebra verifies strict Jensen bias and all-vertex absolute sum, including bridge parity. Sending L/H to zero and Lp to c produces phi(c), and the graph is shortcut-free with probability 1-p tending to one. Independent exact-rational Laplacian elimination and formula checks passed all 1,124 assertions in the included program. This does not assert almost-sure convergence of individual gossip trajectories.

originality.rationale: The inspected primary papers prove harmonic stationary expectations, strong-connectivity concentration for random gossip, community transient behavior, and partial-stubbornness Friedkin-Johnsen concentration. Their precise implications do not include the finite single-shortcut Jensen discrepancy or the critical limit for expected-versus-realized long-time opinions on a connected sparse path with a long detour. The sharp macroscopic all-vertex threshold and its proof were additionally compared against searchable mathematical research records for equivalent formulations. General circuit-reduction literature is an acknowledged ingredient and remains a residual publication-priority risk.
residual_risks: The classical electrical-network literature may contain the same single-link annealed/quenched formula or a dominating abstract perturbation identity not discovered by the queries.

value.rationale: Expected-graph substitution is widely used to model large random social networks. This result supplies a sharp, scale-robust boundary in a fully connected sparse family where even a vanishing-probability additional tie changes expected-network predictions for a positive fraction of all people. The exact limiting error phi(c)/2 (up to 1/4) quantifies macroscopic failure and explains the practical need for connectivity hypotheses, beyond a trivial single-node Jensen inequality.
